summary:
1 John was written to a community that had just split. A group had walked out — "they went out from us," the letter says, "but they did not belong to us" — and those who stayed were shaken, wondering whether they were the ones in the wrong. The writer, working in the tradition of John's Gospel and sharing its vocabulary of light, love, truth, and life, writes to steady them. There is no greeting and no signature; it reads more like a sermon sent to be read aloud than a letter.

The split was over who Jesus is. The departed group had apparently taught that Christ did not truly come in the flesh, an early form of the idea (later called Docetism) that he only seemed human. That is why the letter opens with the senses: "which we have heard, which we have seen with our own eyes, which we have gazed upon and touched with our own hands" (1:1). Against teachers who spiritualized Jesus away, the writer insists the faith rests on a body that could be touched. From there the letter circles, rather than progresses, through three repeating tests of authentic faith: right belief about Jesus, obedience to God's commands, and love for fellow believers. Expect the spiral; it is the letter's structure, not a flaw.

Its most famous lines land harder against this backstory of fracture: "God is light, and in Him there is no darkness at all" (1:5); "God is love" (4:8); "perfect love drives out fear" (4:18); "We love because He first loved us" (4:19). And its purpose is stated outright near the end: "so that you may know that you have eternal life" (5:13). The letter is written to give assurance, and every test it poses serves that end.
